title: NASA Human Research Program
description: NASA Human Research Program overview of research to protect astronaut health and performance in space.
content: NASA's Human Research Program uses ground research facilities, the International Space Station, Artemis missions, and analog environments to develop methods that protect astronaut health and performance.

title: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
description: NASA evidence summary on weight-bearing bone changes in microgravity and mitigation research.
content: NASA reports average bone-density loss of 1% to 1.5% per month during four-to-six-month missions. The page describes exercise and bone scans as parts of monitoring and countermeasure research; these population-level observations do not diagnose an individual.

title: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload
description: NASA Human Health and Performance risk page on sleep quantity and quality, circadian disruption, fatigue, and task performance.
content: NASA describes adequate sleep quantity and quality as important for cognitive performance. The page reports that sleep deprivation and circadian disturbances during spaceflight can contribute to fatigue and task errors, while environmental conditions can affect sleep and well-being.

title: About the Space Radiation Element
description: NASA Human Research Program overview of its Space Radiation Element and astronaut health research.
content: NASA's Space Radiation Element characterizes health outcomes associated with space-radiation exposure. Beyond Earth's protective atmosphere, astronauts encounter ionizing radiation from solar particles and galactic cosmic rays; NASA notes that specific human health effects are not fully understood.

title: The Human Body in Space
description: NASA overview of changes in bone, muscle, and body-fluid distribution during spaceflight.
content: NASA describes bone mineral-density loss and muscle-mass loss in microgravity, as well as an upward shift of body fluids that may affect vision. The page presents general spaceflight effects and countermeasures, not astronaut-specific measurements or diagnoses.
